text.p: Using Colorado's natural beauty as a backdrop, President Bill Clinton courted the state's voters on Saturday as his campaign aides downplayed a rift among Republican strategists over attacking his character.

"In this great debate that we are having here, much more is at stake than whether I become president ... what is really at stake here is what our country will look like as we start into that new century," Clinton said.

In remarks to about 10,000 supporters at the Red Rocks Amphitheater, a concert site erected among ancient rock formations, Clinton promoted his record -- particularly his environmental policies. Before leaving Washington earlier in the day, Clinton signed the Water Resources Development Act, which restores and protects the Florida Everglades.

Clinton planned to fly to New Mexico on Sunday to gather with senior advisers and confidants in Albuquerque and prepare for his final debate on Wednesday with Republican Bob Dole -- who left the campaign trail this weekend and returned to Washington to assess ways to revive his faltering campaign.

Dole's first debate with Clinton and the vice presidential exchange between Al Gore and Jack Kemp has done little to give the Republican campaign momentum. Clinton appears to be maintaining his double-digit lead in most public opinion polls.

With the final presidential debate set for Wednesday in San Diego, Republican strategists have been arguing over using more aggressive tactics to close the gap between the incumbent and the challenger -- with some urging Dole to attack Clinton's character.

Former Education Secretary William Bennett, vice chairman of Dole's campaign and the best-selling author of "The Book of Virtues," has been challenging Clinton's character and urging the Republican nominee to do the same.
Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart criticised Bennett's tactics, saying: "I must have missed the chapter in his book where spite, envy, hostility and negativity are virtues."

Clinton, hounded by questions about marital infidelity and his role in the Whitewater land deal, has not faced many direct attacks on his character by Dole. Many Republican loyalists were disappointed that Kemp did not attack Clinton in the vice presidential debate.

"I think Bob Dole knows what Bob Dole wants to do at this point," said Lockhart, suggesting that the publicity about the internal debate helped the Republican cause by getting journalists to write about allegations involving the president.
"They have no message," Lockhart said. "They have nothing else to talk about, so they keep the character issue" in the limelight.
Although there has been a push to attack Clinton's character, a Time/CNN survey released on Saturday found that nearly half of registered voters think Dole has already been too negative.
In the poll 49 percent said Dole had engaged in too much negative campaigning, compared to just 22 percent who thought Clinton had attacked his opponents too often.

The same poll of 1,676 registered voters on Oct. 10-11 found that among those likely to vote, 53 percent favoured Clinton, 35 percent favoured Dole, and seven percent said they would cast their vote for Texas billionaire Ross Perot.
